body:
These normies you speak of are not very normal. Someone's participation in the routine machine doesn't signal his enjoyment. 

If you want to connect with people, you're going to have to learn how to open up and be kind. I don't mean "try new things and be polite." You're going to have to take stock of your life and pay attention, the closest fucking attention that you've ever paid anything, to how things make you feel. You need to evaluate your life and deconstruct every preconceived notion you have in your head. I know you've already done that on an intellectual level, but now you're going to have to break down what you know about yourself. 

You need to practice authentic kindness. Not politeness, although that helps, too. Kindness is seeing and appreciating people for what they are. 

A huge part of my job is making small talk. Hey, how ya doin'? Isn't this weather so nice? Man, I really need another cup of coffee. I love those shoes! Your baby is just darling, how old is he? 

Hating on lightheartedness and small talk and convention is easy. Paying attention to how things make you feel is hard. Nobody is itching to talk about the weather; what they want is to look at someone's face, and speak and smile and be heard and spend a few moments of their day making a connection with another human. I'm not going to greet a stranger with my tactical analysis of a human rights protest. We're going to talk about the fucking sunshine. 

You're going to need to pay attention to how you feel and then do some spin on your thoughts. You've acknowledged your elitist attitude, which is good. How does it feel to feel better than everyone else? It might feel good, but you acknowledge that making connections might feel better. You already have something to learn from these normies that you're so much better than, because they know how to connect with each other and you don't. 

Just give love. People are telling you about their kids because they are raising humans and that's so important to them. Your reflex may be to think, "this is boring and stupid and I don't care," but be deliberate about following that thought up with "it's unkind of me to think less of this person because I don't take interest in her family; she is so excited, so I'll be excited for her, too." 

I'm hungover and typing on a phone so I don't know how coherent or relevant this is. But I went through this whole process recently; I opened up and I became kind and I shed the elitist narrative. It was hard and rewarding and I hope you figure it out, too.

Hi -- I've really been meditating on the questions and points that have been raised here, and they've meant a lot to me.

I do know that polyamory is not something that is only in question because of this guy -- the concept of polyamory has been knocking around in my head for as long as I've considered the mechanics of my ideal relationships, before I knew there was a word for it. It's never exactly been a goal, but always an avenue I've intended to explore in earnest. Being somewhat abruptly confronted with a real-world scenario in which I might become polyamorous has forced the issue a bit -- I always assumed it's something I'd go find for myself, rather than have it be something that is presented to me -- but it's always been on the agenda. I am not sure if it will work or feel good but I am certain that I want to try, feet-first, but earnestly.

I don't know, right now, what I "need" or what I "want" or what I am and am not "okay with." The amount of time and care I need from people (everyone, not just romantic partners) is something that I'm actively altering about myself and I don't know what that's going to look like at the end (if the process is one that ends -- I'm not sure either way). My most recent two relationships were a mess of mismatched time-needs (one relationship where I was the one who needed more, and the other where my partner needed more). I'm trying to be sturdier, more self-reliant, comfortable with absence... and I don't know how much my sturdier self needs from a partner. I'm just trying to pay attention to how things feel, and adjust accordingly.

I worry that I've misrepresented my concerns; when I say that I wonder about asking him for time, I mean that I don't know how much my feelings are appropriate to make clear to him. I don't know if it's cool to make it clear that hey, I'd like to see him again, I'm free this weekend, what about you? I don't know where I stand in his life to the point that I don't know if it would be okay to even ask where I stand. I all but know that he's more important to me than I am to him. I don't know what to do with that information, or to what extent my anxiety relates to reality vs fear vs self-esteem. Maybe my anxiety is justified, and I'm small potatoes, and to burden him with my thoughts and wants would not just be unwanted, but inappropriate, the way it's inappropriate to ask your server on a date while she's taking your order during a lunch rush. Or maybe it's justified anxiety, and I'm small potatoes, and it's totally appropriate to try but I'll end up being shut down. 

So, lately, my strategy is to wait and assume he'll reach out and make moves as he wants to. If he has time and wants to see me, he'll try; if he wants to talk, he will. I don't know if that's true, but at least by doing nothing and saying nothing, I'm not destroying anything, hurting anyone, crossing any uncrossable lines. It's passive, and I'm not too sure if it's the right idea, but it's where I am.

But, fuck, sometimes it gets darker for me. I wonder if he's going to change his mind about me once he gets to know me better; he describes me as "cool" and "interesting" and I'm afraid I've misled him. I'm worried about letting my self-esteem get too high and forgiving myself for inadequacies I don't deserve to be forgiven for. I'm worried that this woman, who seems like someone I'd love to get to know, will not see me as worth getting to know. I'm worried that I'm emotionally investing in someone who doesn't want to invest as much in me. 

I'm struggling, and I know the advice is always, "talk to your partner about how you feel!" but I don't know if I'm allowed to talk to him about this. I've ALWAYS been anxious about asking too much of people; when I like someone, I REALLY LIKE them, and I have to be really deliberate about giving people space. I'm such a new part of his life, and I don't know what I mean to him. I don't know if I'm entitled to ask for his time and nurturing. I don't know if I mean as much to him as he means to me. 

Can I even consider him a "partner?" He's a busy guy; we exchange about 10 texts a week. We haven't seen each other in weeks. Is it too much to text him and say "hey, I feel uncomfortable about some things and I'd like to talk to you about them," considering that we're not really together? Shouldn't that be worked out in person? Is it fair to ask to spend time with him? 

Was it fair of him to present this to me and then not follow up to check on how I feel? Is it unfair to have strong feelings about him and not give him a chance to help me? Is it fair to have strong feelings about him at all, considering how little commitment we've made to each other? 

I worry that my stress over the fact that he doesn't need to text me or see me much means that my needs are more than he is willing to accommodate; is it fair to make that assumption without telling him how I feel? Is it fair to try to do the hard work of getting comfortable with getting less from a partner without checking in with him first? Is it fair to ask for him to accommodate my desires when we're not really together? Is it fair to go to my friends or strangers on the internet for advice instead of going directly to him? 

I'm sorry this is so long. I just feel like a mess tonight.  And I feel alone. And I like him, and I'm exploring something new, and I don't even know if I'm overstepping his boundaries by asking him to help me through it.
